findings.paper_title: SM 2627 Q1 TM Update App A 21-07-26
findings.headline: Investment income £100k short of budget (16% shortfall) as portfolio depleted for internal borrowing
findings.detail: The council budgeted £626,130 in investment income for 2026/27 expecting rate decreases, but rates have remained higher and the investment portfolio has been reduced as the council used cash balances for internal borrowing instead of external debt. This combination produces a £100k shortfall forecast, reducing internal funding capacity for capital programmes.
findings.matters: Lower investment income reduces the council's internal funding sources for capital projects and increases reliance on higher-cost external borrowing, compounding the effect of elevated interest rates
findings.figures: £626,130 budgeted investment income vs £100,000 shortfall forecast
findings.quote: A shortfall of £100,000 is forecast against this budget

findings.paper_title: SM 2627 Q1 TM Update App A 21-07-26
findings.headline: Council taking 6-month borrowing and using internal cash reserves to avoid locking in high rates
findings.detail: Rather than committing to medium or long-term external borrowing at current elevated PWLB rates, the council took a £5m loan for only 6 months at 4.25% in April and continues relying on temporary internal borrowing from cash reserves. This strategy defers borrowing decisions pending potential future rate decreases but creates refinancing risk if rates remain high.
findings.matters: Short-term borrowing and internal borrowing defer capital funding certainty and expose the council to material refinancing risk when existing loans mature, particularly if interest rates remain elevated
findings.figures: £5m 6-month loan at 4.25% taken April 2026; forecast year-end external borrowing £17m; PWLB rates 5.00% (5-year) and 5.50% (10-year)
findings.quote: Temporary internal borrowing continues for the remainder of the CFR whilst intra-local authority external borrowing interest rates are high.

findings.paper_title: SM 2627 Q1 TM Update App A 21-07-26
findings.headline: Opening Capital Financing Requirement £2.3m higher than Treasury Strategy estimate
findings.detail: The CFR (total capital expenditure not yet funded) was revised upward from the Treasury Management Strategy Statement estimate of £13.718m to £16.042m based on 2025/26 provisional outturn. This £2.3m increase indicates the council's underlying capital financing need exceeded prior projections. Closing CFR is forecast at £27.006m.
findings.matters: Material upward revision in CFR indicates worsening capital financing need and trajectory toward higher debt levels, affecting long-term borrowing sustainability
findings.figures: Opening CFR £13.718m (TMSS estimate) vs £16.042m (current); Closing CFR £27.006m
findings.quote: The CFR represents the total outstanding capital expenditure which has not yet been paid for from either revenue or capital resources. It is essentially a measure of the Council's underlying need to borrow to finance capital expenditure

findings.paper_title: SM 2627 Q1 TM Update App A 21-07-26
findings.headline: Bank rate forecast unchanged at 3.75% for full year; budget assumed cuts to 3.25%
findings.detail: The budget was set expecting two rate decreases during 2026/27 (to 3.50% by end of Q1 and 3.25% by Q3), but the Bank of England base rate has remained at 3.75% since year start with no cuts forecast. PWLB borrowing rates are similarly higher than budgeted, restricting opportunities for medium to long-term external borrowing.
findings.matters: Persistent higher interest rates increase debt service costs and constrain the council's ability to refinance debt or fund capital programmes at budgeted rates
findings.figures: Bank Rate 3.75% (unchanged); PWLB 5-year rate 5.00%, 10-year rate 5.50%
findings.quote: The budget was set with the assumption that there would be two decreases during the year, to 3.50% by the end of quarter 1 and 3.25% by the end of quarter 3.

findings.paper_title: Annual Governance Statement
findings.headline: Council ceased discretionary Carelink service in September 2026 after being unable to maintain safe staffing levels
findings.detail: Council identified significant risks in providing safe Carelink (monitoring service) due to staffing shortages. Efforts to recruit and retain staff, including considering agency options, were unsuccessful. In June 2026, council decided to end the service with managed wind-down by September 2026. Residents being helped to find alternative providers.
findings.matters: Service closure shows the council cannot sustain certain services with available staffing and resources, indicating operational and potentially financial constraints
findings.figures: Decision made June 2026; service ended September 2026
findings.quote: In June 2026, the Council took the decision to cease the provision of the service, with a managed wind down to September 2026.

findings.paper_title: Annual Governance Statement
findings.headline: Council established reserve for LGR costs which has been drawn down and replenished; future government funding changes uncertain
findings.detail: A dedicated reserve was created to fund LGR costs and has been 'replenished' (indicating it was drawn down during the year and refilled). LGR will bring changes to central government funding. Negative funding impacts in 2026/27 are mitigated by one-off government grants, but future funding remains uncertain.
findings.matters: Council is relying on reserves to fund reorganization costs while facing potential funding headwinds from 2027/28 onward, reducing financial flexibility and resilience
findings.figures: Reserve replenished during 2025/26; one-off grants for 2026/27 only
findings.quote: A reserve to fund the costs of LGR was established and replenished and is monitored regularly.

findings.paper_title: Annual Governance Statement
findings.headline: LGR will create increasing costs through April 2028 vesting day
findings.detail: The council has already incurred modest costs for LGR preparation and expects these to increase substantially as vesting day approaches. These costs include legacy programme costs associated with the wind-down of the current council.
findings.matters: A lender needs to understand the scale and trajectory of reorganization costs affecting the council's financial position over the next 20 months
findings.figures: Costs increasing through period to April 2028; legacy programme in transformation planning
findings.quote: We expect there to be costs of LGR and have been incurring some modest costs already with this expected to increase as vesting day is approached.

findings.paper_title: Annual Governance Statement
findings.headline: Local Government Reorganisation will merge High Peak into new entities by April 2028; government decision on configuration expected July 2026
findings.detail: Government announced LGR in December 2024. Five local government configurations were submitted for Derbyshire. The council's current Alliance with Staffordshire Moorlands District Council will end 31 March 2028 when new entities become operational 1 April 2028 (vesting day). At the meeting date (28 July 2026), the government had just reached or was about to announce the preferred configuration.
findings.matters: Major structural change over the next 20 months affecting the council's operations, partnerships, governance framework and financial arrangements; final shape still uncertain
findings.figures: Government decision July 2026; Alliance ends 31 March 2028; vesting day 1 April 2028
findings.quote: the Council's Alliance with Staffordshire Moorlands District Council is expected to end on 31 March 2028 as new entities become operational on 1 April 2028 (vesting day).

findings.paper_title: Treasury Management Update Q1 2026/27
findings.headline: HRA borrowing costs forecast to overspend by £30,910
findings.detail: The Housing Revenue Account is forecasting an overspend of £30,910 on borrowing costs, while the general fund underspends by £11,740. The imbalance indicates cost pressures within the HRA's debt servicing.
findings.matters: Overspends on HRA borrowing costs are a direct hit to housing revenue and may signal rising debt servicing costs or higher than anticipated borrowing across the housing account.
findings.figures: £30,910 HRA overspend; £11,740 general fund underspend; total debt £74.3m; average borrowing rate 3.92%
findings.quote: Borrowing costs on the general fund are forecast to be underspent by £11,740 on the general fund and overspent by £30,910 on the HRA.

findings.paper_title: Treasury Management Update Q1 2026/27
findings.headline: Investment income forecast to shortfall by £165,860 against plan
findings.detail: The council is forecasting a shortfall of £165,860 in investment income for 2026/27, split between £74,560 on the general fund and £91,300 on the HRA. The shortfall against budgeted income is driven by average investment balances of £14.9m against the budgeted assumption.
findings.matters: Investment income is non-service revenue that offsets council costs; a shortfall of this size indicates either lower cash balances than anticipated or lower returns on deposits, both material to the council's cashflow and reserve position.
findings.figures: £165,860 total shortfall (£74,560 general fund, £91,300 HRA); average investment balances £14.9m
findings.quote: A shortfall of £165,860 (£74,560 general fund, £91,300 HRA) in investment income is forecast.

findings.paper_title: HPBC - Risk Management Update (28.07.2026)
findings.headline: AES subsidiary has 9 high-rated risks creating material company-level exposure
findings.detail: The council's wholly owned company AES carries 9 high-rated risks alongside 5 medium-rated risks. This represents substantial risk concentration within a council-controlled entity. The specific risks are detailed in Appendix F.
findings.matters: Council-controlled companies represent contingent liability; high risk exposure in a major subsidiary (AES) signals potential for council financial exposure or need for support
findings.figures: AES: 9 high, 5 medium risks; Alliance Norse: 2 high risks; MyActive: 1 medium, 20 low risks
findings.quote: The review of the Council Controlled Company risk registers has identified 11 risks that are currently rated as 'high' and therefore above the Council's risk tolerance threshold... AES: 9 high, 5 medium rated risks

findings.paper_title: HPBC - Risk Management Update (28.07.2026)
findings.headline: Local Government Reorganisation creating six high-rated governance and financial risks
findings.detail: The council is managing 6 risks specifically arising from potential local government reorganisation. These relate directly to governance continuity, workforce capacity, and financial planning during an uncertain period of potential structural change.
findings.matters: LGR uncertainty creates risk around service continuity, decision-making authority, and financial planning stability; lenders need to understand how management is handling this strategic uncertainty
findings.figures: 6 high-rated LGR-specific risks identified
findings.quote: The June 2026 review of the LGR risk register identifies 6 risks that are currently rated as 'high' and therefore above the Council's risk tolerance threshold. These risks reflect the uncertainty and complexity associated with the reorganisation process, including the need to maintain effective services and governance arrangements while preparing for potential changes to structures, resources, responsibilities and future delivery models.

findings.paper_title: HPBC - Risk Management Update (28.07.2026)
findings.headline: Capital investment and major project risks rated high across 21 of 75 projects
findings.detail: The council has identified 21 project-level risks as high across 11 active programmes, including accelerated housing delivery, Glossop Halls, Buxton Opera House, Victoria Halls, and housing system replacement. Projects represent significant capital deployment and delivery risk.
findings.matters: Major projects can consume significant reserves and create budget pressure if they slip or overrun; lenders track delivery track record and capital discipline
findings.figures: 21 of 75 project risks (28%) rated high; 42 medium (56%); 12 low (16%)
findings.quote: The project risk registers reveal that the Council has identified and assessed 75 project risks in total, of which 21 are rated as 'high' and therefore above the Council's risk tolerance thresholds.

findings.paper_title: HPBC - Risk Management Update (28.07.2026)
findings.headline: HRA Business Plan flagged as high-rated risk
findings.detail: The council's Housing Revenue Account business plan is one of the strategic risks rated as high. This covers housing finance and housing-related service delivery. Details of the specific risk are in Appendix A.
findings.matters: HRA financial health is a material credit consideration; a weak business plan signals pressure on housing investment or service sustainability
findings.figures: 1 of 11 high-rated strategic risks identified
findings.quote: The Council has identified and assessed 23 strategic risks, of which 48% are rated as 'high' and therefore above the Council's risk tolerance threshold. The eleven 'high' rated risks are listed in full at Appendix A.

findings.paper_title: HPBC - Risk Management Update (28.07.2026)
findings.headline: Medium Term Financial Plan identified as high-rated strategic risk
findings.detail: The council's medium-term financial planning is flagged among risks rated 'high' and exceeding risk tolerance thresholds. This is core to understanding whether the council has a credible financial strategy over the coming years. The specific nature of the MTFP risk is detailed in Appendix A.
findings.matters: Lenders need assurance that the council has identified and is actively managing the risks to its financial sustainability over three to five years
findings.figures: 11 of 23 strategic risks (48%) rated as high
findings.quote: The latest analysis of the Strategic Risk Register reveals that the Council has identified and assessed 23 strategic risks, of which 48% are rated as 'high' and therefore above the Council's risk tolerance threshold.

findings.paper_title: Annual Treasury Management Report 2025/26
findings.headline: Council increased external debt by £5 million, reaching £69.3 million
findings.detail: External debt at year-end was £69.3 million, up £5 million net during 2025/26 from several loan maturities and new local authority short-term borrowing. This increase funded capital expenditure of £5.674 million (£4.551 million general fund, £1.123 million HRA). The Executive Director confirms borrowing was only for capital purposes and the statutory authorised limit was not breached.
findings.matters: The direction and composition of debt matters to lenders assessing balance-sheet strength and borrowing trajectory. Confirmation that statutory limits are respected is a baseline governance checkpoint.
findings.figures: External debt £69.3 million; net increase £5 million; capital borrowing need £5.674 million (£4.551m general fund, £1.123m HRA)
findings.quote: External debt at 31 March 2026 was £69.3million including loans from Public Works Loan Board, Market Loans and Local Authority Loans. There were several maturities and new local authority short term loans during the year with a net increase of £5million.

findings.paper_title: Annual Treasury Management Report 2025/26
findings.headline: Investment income fell short of budget by £76,981
findings.detail: The council held an average investment portfolio of £20.3 million across six institutions yielding 3.78% average return, but achieved £76,981 less income than budgeted. This may reflect either lower interest rates achieved than forecast or portfolio balances lower than planned.
findings.matters: Investment income is often relied upon to bridge budget gaps; shortfalls erode financial headroom. Lenders care whether investment assumptions in the budget are conservative or optimistic.
findings.figures: £20.3 million average portfolio held; 3.78% average return; £76,981 shortfall against general fund budget
findings.quote: A provisional shortfall of £76,981 is reported against the general fund budget.

findings.paper_title: Annual Treasury Management Report 2025/26
findings.headline: Borrowing costs exceeded budget by £160,497 in 2025/26
findings.detail: The council's actual borrowing costs were £160,497 over the budgeted amount. With external debt of £69.3 million held at year-end, this suggests either higher-than-forecast interest rates or additional borrowing not anticipated. The council holds loans from PWLB, market lenders, and other local authorities.
findings.matters: A finance director needs to understand why treasury cost forecasts diverged from actuals; this determines whether budget planning for future years requires adjustment. Lenders assess a council's ability to forecast and manage debt-service costs accurately.
findings.figures: £160,497 overspent; external debt £69.3 million; net increase in debt £5 million during the year
findings.quote: Provisional overall borrowing costs are £160,497 overspent against the budget.

findings.paper_title: 202526 Medium Term Financial Plan Budget Setting_v1, 02/02/2026 Corporate Select Committee, 12/02/2026 The Executive
findings.headline: High Peak Borough Council will cease to exist in 2029/30 under Local Government Reorganisation
findings.detail: Section 3.6 notes that the final two years of the MTFP (2028/29 and 2029/30) fall outside the life of High Peak Borough Council, which will merge into a new Unitary Authority. The council includes these years in planning but explicitly states "The new Unitary Authority will be responsible for setting the budget for these years."
findings.matters: A lender cannot assume the borrowing entity will exist to service debt beyond 2029/30. Reorganisations carry integration risks, service disruption, and loss of institutional knowledge. Any debt maturing after the merger requires guarantees from the successor authority.
findings.figures: Reorganisation takes effect 2029/30; 2028/29 and 2029/30 are memorandum years only
findings.quote: the last two years of the MTFP (2028/29 and 2029/30) will fall outside the life of High Peak Borough Council

findings.paper_title: 202526 Medium Term Financial Plan Budget Setting_v1, 02/02/2026 Corporate Select Committee, 12/02/2026 The Executive
findings.headline: Budget forecasts for 2029/30 assume net use of reserves to achieve balance
findings.detail: Section 3.10 states the forecast predicts a balanced budget position by 2029/30 "with a net use of reserves." This means reserves will be consumed to maintain budget balance in the final year of the current council's operation.
findings.matters: Reserves drawn down to balance a budget suggest structural deficits that cannot be funded from revenue. This is a red flag: if the council cannot balance its budget from income in its final year, it signals either service reductions or reserve depletion.
findings.figures: Plan shows balanced budget 2029/30 only with reserve drawdown
findings.quote: The forecast predicts a balanced budget position by 2029/30 with a net use of reserves

findings.paper_title: 202526 Medium Term Financial Plan Budget Setting_v1, 02/02/2026 Corporate Select Committee, 12/02/2026 The Executive
findings.headline: MTFP for 2027/28 and 2028/29 flagged as subject to greater uncertainty and risk
findings.detail: The paper explicitly states the 2026/27 budget is balanced but is followed by "greater uncertainty and risk in the MTFP for future years." The council cannot confidently forecast beyond the coming year despite presenting a four-year plan.
findings.matters: A lender relies on councils being able to forecast and manage through predictable cycles. Explicit uncertainty in years 2-4 of a four-year plan suggests the council is uncertain about income, costs, or both.
findings.figures: Plan runs 2026/27 to 2029/30; uncertainty flagged for years 2-4
findings.quote: a balanced 2026/27 budget on both the revenue and capital side, but with greater uncertainty and risk in the MTFP for future years

findings.paper_title: 202526 Medium Term Financial Plan Budget Setting_v1, 02/02/2026 Corporate Select Committee, 12/02/2026 The Executive
findings.headline: Council anticipated greater costs than originally forecast due to inflation drag and funding cuts
findings.detail: Section 3.7 explicitly states that the Council will incur greater costs than anticipated when the MTFP was set the previous year, attributable to funding cuts and the cumulative effect of inflation drag on council budgets. This indicates the council is revising costs upward mid-plan.
findings.matters: Cost inflation exceeding budget forecasts erodes the real value of any balanced budget. It signals that the council's cost base is growing faster than projected, which affects debt servicing capacity in future years.
findings.figures: No specific figure given for the variance
findings.quote: it is anticipated the Council will incur greater costs than anticipated originally in setting the MTFP last year as a result of the funding cuts and effects of inflation 'drag' on Council budgets

findings.paper_title: 202526 Medium Term Financial Plan Budget Setting_v1, 02/02/2026 Corporate Select Committee, 12/02/2026 The Executive
findings.headline: Employer's National Insurance grant funding fell significantly short of actual costs in 2025/26
findings.detail: The paper notes that while the pay award for 2025/26 was largely in line with budget assumptions, the Employer's National Insurance grant funding the Council received fell significantly short of actual costs incurred. This represents a structural mismatch between government grant assumptions and council reality.
findings.matters: A lender needs confidence that government funding assumptions are reliable. A significant shortfall in a mandatory employment cost shows councils cannot rely on published grant forecasts and must absorb gaps from elsewhere.
findings.figures: Not quantified in the summary; appears in the cost pressures discussion
findings.quote: the amount of Employer's National Insurance grant funding the Council received fell significantly short of the costs actually incurred

findings.paper_title: Appendix B for 202526 Medium Term Financial Plan Budget Setting
findings.headline: HRA housing stock condition surveys restarted only in 2024/25 after a seven-year gap, with rolling 5-year cycle of survey.
findings.detail: The last full housing stock condition surveys were undertaken in 2017. A 5-year rolling programme began in 2024/25 to survey 20% of stock each year to provide updated cost projections over 30 years for maintenance, Decent Homes Standard and energy rating improvements. HRA capital spend is forecast at £46.1 million over five years, but cost projections are based on partial and aging survey data.
findings.matters: A seven-year gap in full surveys means the council's current HRA maintenance liability may be significantly understated. As surveys complete, unexpected cost increases could force sudden capital or reserve drawdowns.
findings.figures: HRA total programme £46,127,930 over 2025/26–2029/30; rolling 20% survey per year commenced 2024/25
findings.quote: The last full housing stock conditions surveys were undertaken in 2017. A 5-year programme of new surveys commenced in 2024/25 and provision has been made in the budget to survey 20% of the stock each year in a rolling programme to provide updated cost projections over the next 30 years.

findings.paper_title: Appendix B for 202526 Medium Term Financial Plan Budget Setting
findings.headline: Leisure centre investment needs remain unsolved for Glossop, with major refurbishment ongoing at New Mills.
findings.detail: A Future Leisure Provision review concluded that major investment was needed to upgrade leisure facilities across the borough. New Mills Leisure Centre refurbishment is 'now in progress,' but Glossop's leisure centre provision still needs 'a workable solution' to be found. The capital programme includes £5.26 million for leisure spend over five years, but the Glossop solution remains undefined.
findings.matters: Undefined solutions to service provision often precede budget overruns or sudden capital calls. Ongoing major refurbishment at New Mills and the absence of a plan for Glossop create delivery and cost risk.
findings.quote: Major projects that emerged from the review included significant refurbishments work at New Mills Leisure Centre, which is now in progress; and the need to find a workable solution to the issue of leisure centre provision in Glossop.

findings.paper_title: Appendix B for 202526 Medium Term Financial Plan Budget Setting
findings.headline: The council is significantly under-borrowing relative to its Capital Financing Requirement, reliant on internal cash reserves.
findings.detail: The council's gross debt is forecast at £72.96 million in 2026/27, but its Capital Financing Requirement is £108.79 million—meaning it is under-borrowing by £35.8 million. The council is using internal cash balances to bridge this gap rather than external borrowing, a decision it is keeping 'under careful review' because it is 'balancing temporary availability of cash reserves with interest rate forecasts.'
findings.matters: This strategy depends on interest rates falling towards the end of the MTFP. If rates remain elevated longer than forecast, the council's reserves will deplete faster and it will face higher external borrowing costs when it eventually needs to borrow.
findings.figures: Gross Debt 2026/27: £72,961k; CFR 2026/27: £108,787k; (under)/over borrowing: -£35,826k
findings.quote: Alternatively, 'internal borrowing' (the use of cash balances) could be used temporarily, particularly in the current interest rate climate where borrowing rates are high and predicted to fall towards the end of the MTFP. This is kept under careful review balancing temporary availability of cash reserves with interest rate forecasts.

findings.paper_title: Appendix B for 202526 Medium Term Financial Plan Budget Setting
findings.headline: Local Government Reorganisation will end the Strategic Alliance with Staffordshire Moorlands on 31 March 2028, requiring dismantlement planning.
findings.detail: The council's joint management structure and shared services with Staffordshire Moorlands District Council will cease on 31 March 2028 due to LGR. The council must plan for dismantlement of the Alliance in that timeframe. Until then, joint arrangements remain the means of service delivery. The Borough Plan is being refocused within the context of LGR.
findings.matters: An unplanned or poorly-managed separation could create service delivery disruption, unbudgeted transition costs, or sudden loss of efficiency savings that the council currently relies on.
findings.figures: Strategic Alliance dismantlement required by 31 March 2028
findings.quote: The implications of LGR mean that this arrangement will come to an end on 31 March 2028 and the Council must plan for the dismantlement of the Alliance in that timeframe.

findings.paper_title: Appendix B for 202526 Medium Term Financial Plan Budget Setting
findings.headline: Multiple structural and health & safety issues across the council's operational property portfolio require investment.
findings.detail: A condition survey identified that a number of operational assets are dated in appearance, there are structural issues requiring correction, several health and safety works need to be carried out, and investment is needed in electrical and mechanical infrastructure in multiple buildings. The 30-year Asset Management Plan shows £10.5 million to be spent on the general fund property portfolio in the five-year MTFP.
findings.matters: Unforeseen structural or safety defects can lead to emergency capital spend or service disruption. Deferred maintenance liabilities that exceed forecasts are a credit risk signal.
findings.figures: £10,521,870 Asset Management spend over 2025/26–2029/30; includes £5,217,960 in 2026/27 alone
findings.quote: There are structural issues associated with a number of the Council's buildings that require correction. There are a several health and safety related works that need to be carried out.

findings.paper_title: Appendix B for 202526 Medium Term Financial Plan Budget Setting
findings.headline: Nutrient neutrality is delaying planned land disposals that fund the capital programme.
findings.detail: The council's strategy relies on £9.6 million of capital receipts from land disposals during 2026/27–2029/30. However, nutrient neutrality rules around the River Wye drainage basin have already caused delays to 'several' intended disposals in recent years. The council acknowledged in its 2018 land review that it expected to yield £7.4 million over four years from disposals, but timing is now uncertain.
findings.matters: If planned land sales slip, the capital programme's funding gaps widen and the council's ability to fund infrastructure and asset maintenance without additional borrowing becomes constrained.
findings.figures: £9.6 million of capital receipts anticipated from land disposals in MTFP 2026/27–2029/30; original strategy estimated £7.4 million over four years
findings.quote: The issue of nutrient neutrality has led to delays in several of the intended land disposals around the river Wye drainage basin over recent years.

findings.paper_title: High Peak Borough Council - Draft Auditors Annual Report 2024-25
findings.headline: Eight prior-year audit recommendations remain unimplemented, some dating back to 2022/23, including on risk management and governance reporting.
findings.detail: Multiple improvement recommendations spanning governance, financial planning and risk management remain in progress from prior years: detailed savings plan documentation (IR2), RAG-rating of savings (IR3), risk scoring methodology (IR5), monthly AMT financial reporting (IR6), and fraud awareness training for members (IR12), among others. These span 2022/23 through 2023/24, indicating slower-than-expected implementation of audit recommendations.
findings.matters: Slower implementation of audit recommendations can indicate governance challenges or resource constraints in executing management improvements; a lender would monitor this as a potential early indicator of broader execution challenges.
findings.figures: 8 prior-year recommendations carried forward to 2024/25; multiple recommendations from 2022/23 still in progress
findings.quote: there are outstanding recommendations on producing detailed efficiency programmes and alignment with the MTFP and on RAG-rating savings plans as part of reporting to Members which are yet to be implemented. Please see pages 31 and 32

findings.paper_title: High Peak Borough Council - Draft Auditors Annual Report 2024-25
findings.headline: Local Government Reorganisation creates material financial planning uncertainty not yet reflected in the Medium-Term Financial Plan.
findings.detail: The Council is required to submit LGR proposals by 28 November 2025 under a government reorganisation programme. The current MTFP does not include financial projections for the impact of LGR, with the auditor noting there is 'not yet sufficient detail or certainty as to the impact.' Future iterations will need to incorporate these as certainty increases. This is a material uncertainty for medium-term financial planning.
findings.matters: LGR could significantly alter the Council's financial position, service delivery model, and borrowing needs, making current financial forecasts incomplete and potentially unreliable for lending decisions until LGR impact is quantified.
findings.figures: LGR proposals due 28 November 2025; new unitaries to be established April 2028
findings.quote: We note that the MTFP did not include any projections or estimations to reflect potential financial implications of the proposed Local Government Reorganisation as there is not yet sufficient detail or certainty as to the impact. Future iterations of the MTFP will need to incorporate these as certainty increases.

findings.paper_title: High Peak Borough Council - Draft Auditors Annual Report 2024-25
findings.headline: Housing Revenue Account long-term sustainability remains unresolved after multiple years of recommendations.
findings.detail: An improvement recommendation from 2022/23 (IR8) to identify a long-term sustainable solution to balancing the HRA remains in progress and not yet implemented. Whilst the 2024/25 HRA achieved a £0.99m operating surplus against a budgeted deficit of £1.12m and the minimum reserve level has been increased to £3m (£780 per property), the fundamental long-term sustainability of the HRA is still outstanding.
findings.matters: A lender financing a council with significant housing stock needs assurance on the HRA's long-term financial viability; an unresolved multi-year recommendation suggests slower progress on this issue.
findings.figures: HRA minimum reserve increased to £3m; 2024/25 operating surplus of £0.99m
findings.quote: there is an outstanding recommendation on achieving financial balance in the long-term for the HRA that is yet to be implemented

findings.paper_title: High Peak Borough Council - Draft Auditors Annual Report 2024-25
findings.headline: Fire Safety Act compliance at 8.8% of target, against 50% target for door compliance.
findings.detail: The Council's largest performance indicator misalignment is fire doors compliant with the Fire Safety Act 2021, at only 8.8% against a 50% target. The auditor notes the Council is taking action to improve this. This represents a specific compliance gap with potential operational and liability implications.
findings.matters: A lender would be concerned about any material compliance gap, particularly in health and safety, as it could trigger enforcement action, operational disruption, or unexpected costs.
findings.figures: 8.8% actual vs 50% target
findings.quote: The largest off track indicator was around % fire doors compliant with the Fire Safety Act 2021 (8.8% against 50% target). The Council is taking action to improve this.
